milestones.title: HTML to text

functions.name: extract
functions.doc:
Return the main text of an HTML page, one paragraph per line.

Text inside SKIP_TAGS (and everything nested in them) is dropped. A BLOCK_TAGS tag
starts a new line; inline tags (a, b, span) do not break the text. A newline inside the
HTML source is just whitespace, not a line break. Whitespace inside a line is collapsed
to single spaces, lines are stripped, empty lines are removed, and the lines are joined
with "\n". Hint: subclass html.parser.HTMLParser and keep a depth counter for SKIP_TAGS.

milestones.task: Write extract(html). The tag sets SKIP_TAGS and BLOCK_TAGS are given. Return the lines of text joined by "\n", each stripped, with runs of whitespace collapsed to one space and empty lines removed.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks eleven hand cases (inline tags, <br>, list items, nested skipped tags, entities, an empty page, a page that is all footer) and then all 118 crawl pages: no tag, script text, navigation label, footer or sidebar may survive, every line must be stripped and single-spaced, and every article must keep its headline (with & decoded) and at least 50 words.
hints: Subclass HTMLParser. Keep self.skip = 0 and self.out = []. In handle_starttag add one to skip if the tag is in SKIP_TAGS, and append "\n" if it is in BLOCK_TAGS. In handle_endtag subtract one from skip and append a newline for block tags again (so text after a block starts a new line).
In handle_data, when skip == 0, append the text after replacing every run of whitespace (including newlines) with a single space: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", data).
After feed, join the pieces, split on "\n", strip each line, and drop the empty ones.
If "Hello big\n world" comes out as three lines, the raw newline is being treated as a block break.
milestones.solution:
class _Extractor(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)       # & arrives as "&"
        self.skip = 0                                  # how many SKIP_TAGS we are currently inside
        self.out = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip += 1
        if tag in BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.out.append("\n")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in SKIP_TAGS:
            self.skip = max(0, self.skip - 1)
        if tag in BLOCK_TAGS:
            self.out.append("\n")

    def handle_data(self, data):
        if not self.skip:
            self.out.append(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", data))      # a newline in the HTML source is only a space

def extract(html):
    """Return the main text of an HTML page, one paragraph per line.

    Text inside SKIP_TAGS (and everything nested in them) is dropped. A BLOCK_TAGS tag
    starts a new line; inline tags (a, b, span) do not break the text. A newline inside the
    HTML source is just whitespace, not a line break. Whitespace inside a line is collapsed
    to single spaces, lines are stripped, empty lines are removed, and the lines are joined
    with "\\n". Hint: subclass html.parser.HTMLParser and keep a depth counter for SKIP_TAGS.
    """
    parser = _Extractor()
    parser.feed(html)
    parser.close()
    lines = [re.sub(r"\s+", " ", ln).strip() for ln in "".join(parser.out).split("\n")]
    return "\n".join(ln for ln in lines if ln)
milestones.explain:
A crawler gives you the whole page: a head with a title and scripts, a navigation bar, a cookie banner, the article, a sidebar of related stories and a footer. Only the article is worth learning from. The task is called boilerplate removal, and it is harder than it sounds because boilerplate is whatever repeats across a site, and there is no tag that says which part is which. Chapter 1 reported that the choice of extractor changed benchmark scores measurably (FineWeb's authors preferred trafilatura on raw pages to Common Crawl's ready-made text), so this is a modelling decision, not a chore.

Your extractor works on tags, which is crude and good enough for the synthetic crawl. Python's html.parser.HTMLParser calls your methods as it reads: handle_starttag when a tag opens, handle_endtag when it closes and handle_data for the text between. Three details decide whether you get clean text:

  • Skipping needs a depth counter, not a flag. Text inside nav, script, style, head, header, footer and aside is dropped, but skipped tags nest (a nav inside an aside). A True/False flag switches back on at the first closing tag and leaks the rest of the outer element.
  • A newline in the source is only whitespace. HTML authors wrap lines wherever they like. A line break in the output comes from a block tag such as p, div, li or br, never from a newline character inside the text. An inline tag such as b or span must not break the line or add a space: foo<span>bar</span> is foobar.
  • Character references such as & arrive decoded if you create the parser with convert_charrefs=True (the default).

Here is the extractor from the finished solution on one of the stub pages in the crawl, and then on an article (script in exp_peek.py):

$ python3 exp_peek.py
<html><body><nav><a href='/'>Home</a></nav><p>Page not found. Please check the address and try again.</p></body></html>
-> 'Page not found. Please check the address and try again.'

1643 characters of HTML -> 948 characters, 160 words
Courts report 20 & outlook
milestones.card:
A crawled web page is mostly not the article: it also carries menus, scripts and a footer. Extraction keeps only the text a reader would call the article, one paragraph per line.

The parser _Extractor is already in the file: after you feed it the page (and close it), its out list holds text pieces and "\n" markers. Text inside nav, footer, script and similar tags is already dropped. Block tags (p, li, br) add a marker; inline tags (b, span) do not. extract(html) turns that list into clean lines: join the pieces, split at the markers, collapse each run of whitespace to one space, strip each line, drop empty lines and join the rest with "\n". Each piece was collapsed alone, so neighbouring pieces can still leave a double space.

<nav>Menu</nav><p>Hi <b>big</b> world</p><p>Bye</p>
gives "Hi big world\nBye"

Read more: A3 chapter 1, extraction from HTML to prose.

milestones.title: C4 and Gopher quality filters

functions.name: c4_line_filter
functions.doc:
Keep only lines that pass the C4 line rules (Raffel et al., 2020), joined with "\n".

A line is kept if it has at least MIN_LINE_WORDS words, contains none of
BAD_LINE_SUBSTRINGS (compare in lower case), and, when `require_punct` is true, ends
with one of TERMINAL. Chapter 1: FineWeb found the punctuation rule removed about 30%
of all tokens, so the pipeline below switches it off.

functions.name: quality_flags
functions.doc:
Names of the Gopher-style rules the text breaks (empty list = passes), in this order:

length, mean_word_length, symbols, bullets, ellipsis, alpha, stopwords,
repeated_lines, boilerplate

functions.name: keep
functions.doc: True if the text breaks none of the quality rules.

milestones.task: Write c4_line_filter(text, require_punct=True), quality_flags(text) and keep(text). Guard every division so the empty text does not crash.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the C4 rules on a hand-written page (including that "Home" and "Buy now" are too short), a clean 60-word text (no flags), the boundaries (exactly 50 words passes, 40 fails with only length), one text built to break each of the other rules, the flag order, and then the crawl: every spam, stub and non-English page must be dropped, every article and copy kept, and the three short good notes dropped.
hints: Split the text with text.split() for words and text.split("\n") for lines. Use max(1, len(...)) as the denominator for every ratio.
str.endswith accepts a tuple, so line.endswith(TERMINAL) works. Compare BAD_LINE_SUBSTRINGS against line.lower().
Symbol ratio: sum(w.count("#") + w.count("...") for w in words) / len(words).
Alphabetic words: any(c.isalpha() for c in w). Stop words: strip punctuation from each word, lower-case it, intersect with STOPWORDS and compare the size of the intersection with MIN_STOPWORDS.
Duplicate-line fraction: (len(lines) - len(set(lines))) / len(lines).
milestones.solution:
def c4_line_filter(text, require_punct=True):
    """Keep only lines that pass the C4 line rules (Raffel et al., 2020), joined with "\\n".

    A line is kept if it has at least MIN_LINE_WORDS words, contains none of
    BAD_LINE_SUBSTRINGS (compare in lower case), and, when `require_punct` is true, ends
    with one of TERMINAL. Chapter 1: FineWeb found the punctuation rule removed about 30%
    of all tokens, so the pipeline below switches it off.
    """
    kept = []
    for line in text.split("\n"):
        line = line.strip()
        if len(line.split()) < MIN_LINE_WORDS:
            continue
        if any(bad in line.lower() for bad in BAD_LINE_SUBSTRINGS):
            continue
        if require_punct and not line.endswith(TERMINAL):
            continue
        kept.append(line)
    return "\n".join(kept)

def quality_flags(text):
    """Names of the Gopher-style rules the text breaks (empty list = passes), in this order:

        length, mean_word_length, symbols, bullets, ellipsis, alpha, stopwords,
        repeated_lines, boilerplate
    """
    words = text.split()
    lines = [ln for ln in text.split("\n") if ln.strip()]
    n_words, n_lines = max(1, len(words)), max(1, len(lines))
    flags = []
    if not MIN_WORDS <= len(words) <= MAX_WORDS:
        flags.append("length")
    mean_len = sum(len(w) for w in words) / n_words
    if not MIN_MEAN_WORD <= mean_len <= MAX_MEAN_WORD:
        flags.append("mean_word_length")
    if sum(w.count("#") + w.count("...") for w in words) / n_words > MAX_SYMBOL_RATIO:
        flags.append("symbols")
    if sum(ln.lstrip().startswith(BULLETS) for ln in lines) / n_lines > MAX_BULLET_LINES:
        flags.append("bullets")
    if sum(ln.rstrip().endswith("...") for ln in lines) / n_lines > MAX_ELLIPSIS_LINES:
        flags.append("ellipsis")
    if sum(any(c.isalpha() for c in w) for w in words) / n_words < MIN_ALPHA_WORDS:
        flags.append("alpha")
    present = {w.strip(".,;:!?\"'()").lower() for w in words} & STOPWORDS
    if len(present) < MIN_STOPWORDS:
        flags.append("stopwords")
    if (len(lines) - len(set(lines))) / n_lines > MAX_DUPLICATE_LINES:
        flags.append("repeated_lines")
    low = text.lower()
    if "lorem ipsum" in low or "{" in text:
        flags.append("boilerplate")
    return flags

def keep(text):
    """True if the text breaks none of the quality rules."""
    return not quality_flags(text)
milestones.explain:
Extraction gives you text. Quality filtering decides whether it is worth keeping, using rules cheap enough to run on every page. This milestone implements two families that chapter 1 described.

C4 line rules (Raffel et al., 2020, the T5 paper) work on single lines. A line survives if it has at least a few words, contains none of a list of giveaway strings (javascript, cookie, terms of use, privacy policy) and, optionally, ends in terminal punctuation. The punctuation rule is the interesting one: chapter 1 reported that FineWeb's authors found it gave the biggest single boost on a benchmark and also removed about 30 percent of all tokens, so you will write it as an option (require_punct) and the pipeline will switch it off.

Gopher style document rules (Rae et al., 2021, whose pipeline FineWeb and others reuse) work on the whole text and are statistical. Your quality_flags returns the names of the rules a text breaks, so a dropped page always comes with a reason:

FlagFires whenTypical culprit
lengthfewer than 50 or more than 100,000 wordsstubs such as "Page not found"
mean_word_lengthmean word length outside 3 to 10 charactersURL dumps, minified code
symbolsmore than 0.1 of # and ... per wordhashtag and ellipsis stuffing
bulletsmore than 90% of lines start with a bulletproduct lists, link farms
ellipsismore than 30% of lines end with ...truncated snippets
alphafewer than 80% of words contain a lettertables of numbers, gibberish
stopwordsfewer than two distinct words from {the, be, to, of, and, that, have, with}non-English text, keyword lists
repeated_linesmore than 30% of lines are duplicates of another line in the pagetemplated spam
boilerplatecontains "lorem ipsum" or a curly bracketplaceholder text, code and template debris

The stop-word rule is a cheap language identifier: real English contains "the" and "of" almost immediately, and German or Spanish contains none of the eight. The thresholds are given as constants in starter.py so that you and the checker agree on them. Return the flags in the order of the table. Run on the crawl, the finished solution produces this table of which rule fires on which kind of page (script in exp_flags.py):

$ python3 exp_flags.py
kind        pages  kept  rules that fired (pages)
article        40    40  
exact          14    14  
light          13    13  
medium         10    10  
related         6     6  
borderline      3     0  length 3
seo             4     4  
spam           12     0  stopwords 10, repeated_lines 4, boilerplate 2, bullets 2, symbols 2, ellipsis 2, length 2, mean_word_length 2
short           8     0  length 8, stopwords 6
nonenglish      8     0  stopwords 8

Three things stand out. Spam pages usually break several rules at once, as chapter 1 predicted, so the thresholds need no fine tuning. The four keyword-stuffed seo pages pass every rule: they are grammatical English with stop words and no symbols, and only a learned classifier (or a person) would object, which is the reason FineWeb-Edu adds a model after the rules. And the three borderline pages are good text that the 50-word rule discards. A filter is a trade between the junk it removes and the good text it loses; here the loss is three pages, at web scale it is billions of tokens.
milestones.card:
Cheap rules can discard junk before any model reads it. Some judge one line (does it look like a real sentence?), others judge a whole document by simple measurements.

c4_line_filter tests each line against the constants MIN_LINE_WORDS, BAD_LINE_SUBSTRINGS and TERMINAL. quality_flags measures the whole text and returns the names of the rules it breaks, in the docstring's order. In that order the measurements are: word count; mean word length; # and ... per word; share of bullet lines; share of lines ending in ...; share of words with a letter; distinct stop words such as the, of and that (lower-cased, punctuation stripped); share of repeated lines; "lorem ipsum" or {. The thresholds are constants in the file. Guard every division so the empty text is flagged length instead of crashing; keep is true when no flag fires.

"Share this page!" is kept; "Buy now" is dropped (two words)
50 words: no flag.  40 words: ["length"]

Read more: A3 chapter 1, cheap filters first.

milestones.title: exact and line-level deduplication

functions.name: normalise
functions.doc: Lower-case, replace every run of non-alphanumeric characters by one space, strip.

functions.name: exact_dedupe
functions.doc:
Keep the first document of each distinct normalised text.

docs: list of (id, text). Returns (kept, dropped): `kept` is the list of (id, text)
in the original order; `dropped` maps each removed id to the id of the copy it
duplicates. Compare documents by the SHA-256 of normalise(text), not by the text.

functions.name: line_dedupe
functions.doc:
Remove every line that occurs in MORE than `max_docs` different documents.

docs: list of (id, text). Count each line once per document (a line repeated inside
one document still counts once). Returns a new list of (id, text) in the same order;
a document whose lines are all removed keeps its id with the empty text "".

milestones.task: Write normalise(text), exact_dedupe(docs) (returns the kept (id, text) pairs and a dict mapping each removed id to the id it copies) and line_dedupe(docs, max_docs=6).
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand cases: normalisation of a punctuated string; five documents of which three are copies of the first two; a promotional line in five documents with max_docs=4 (removed) and with max_docs=5 (kept, because the rule is "more than"); a line repeated inside one document counts once. Then the crawl: exact_dedupe may only ever merge pages of the same article, line deduplication followed by exact deduplication must find more copies than exact deduplication alone, and at least 13 of the 14 generated exact copies must go.
hints: re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", text.lower()).strip() does the normalisation in one line.
hashlib.sha256(normalise(text).encode()).hexdigest(), and a dict from digest to the first id that had it.
For line_dedupe, a Counter updated with set(text.split("\n")) for every document counts each line once per document. Then rebuild each text from the lines whose count is at most max_docs.
Return a list in the original order, and keep documents that lose every line with the text "".
milestones.solution:
def normalise(text):
    """Lower-case, replace every run of non-alphanumeric characters by one space, strip."""
    return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", " ", text.lower()).strip()

def exact_dedupe(docs):
    """Keep the first document of each distinct normalised text.

    docs: list of (id, text). Returns (kept, dropped): `kept` is the list of (id, text)
    in the original order; `dropped` maps each removed id to the id of the copy it
    duplicates. Compare documents by the SHA-256 of normalise(text), not by the text.
    """
    seen, kept, dropped = {}, [], {}
    for doc_id, text in docs:
        digest = hashlib.sha256(normalise(text).encode()).hexdigest()
        if digest in seen:
            dropped[doc_id] = seen[digest]
        else:
            seen[digest] = doc_id
            kept.append((doc_id, text))
    return kept, dropped

def line_dedupe(docs, max_docs=6):
    """Remove every line that occurs in MORE than `max_docs` different documents.

    docs: list of (id, text). Count each line once per document (a line repeated inside
    one document still counts once). Returns a new list of (id, text) in the same order;
    a document whose lines are all removed keeps its id with the empty text "".
    """
    in_docs = Counter()
    for _, text in docs:
        in_docs.update(set(text.split("\n")))
    return [(i, "\n".join(ln for ln in text.split("\n") if in_docs[ln] <= max_docs)) for i, text in docs]
milestones.explain:
The web repeats itself: mirrors, syndicated articles, pasted licences and templates. Duplicates cost twice, once in wasted compute and once in memorisation (Lee et al., 2021, whose numbers chapter 1 quotes). Two cheap methods come before the expensive one.

Exact deduplication hashes each document and keeps the first of every hash. The trap is what you hash. The hash of the raw text changes if one character does, so two copies of an article that differ in capitalisation, spacing or a trailing exclamation mark look unrelated. Hashing a normalised text (lower-cased, punctuation and whitespace runs reduced to one space) catches those, at no real cost. Use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 so that accidental collisions are not a worry (see applied cryptography for what makes a hash collision-resistant).

Line-level deduplication removes lines that appear in many different documents. "Subscribe to our newsletter for weekly updates." is a perfectly good English sentence and carries no information; it turns up on thousands of otherwise unrelated pages. Llama 3's pipeline, following ccNet, removes lines that occur more than 6 times within each bucket of 30 million documents (chapter 1). Your version counts, for every distinct line, in how many documents it occurs, and deletes the lines over a threshold.

The order matters, and the checker measures it. In the crawl, some pages carry a promotional line in the body and their exact copies carry a different one. Hashing the texts as they are finds only a handful of copies; removing the shared promotional lines first lets exact deduplication see through them.
milestones.card:
The web repeats itself, and training on the same text twice wastes compute and encourages memorising it. Two cheap defences: compare short fingerprints (hashes) of whole documents instead of their text, and delete lines that appear in many different documents.

normalise lower-cases the text and turns every run of non-alphanumeric characters into one space, so copies that differ only in capitals or punctuation get the same fingerprint: hash the normalised text, never the raw text. exact_dedupe(docs) keeps the first document for each fingerprint, in the original order, and also returns a dict from each removed id to the id it copies. line_dedupe counts the documents each distinct line appears in (a line repeated inside one document counts once) and removes lines found in more than max_docs documents. A document left with no lines stays in the list, with "".

normalise("THE  cat!") == normalise("The cat.") == "the cat"
a line in 5 documents: removed at max_docs=4, kept at max_docs=5

Read more: A3 chapter 1, deduplication.

milestones.title: shingles and MinHash

functions.name: shingles
functions.doc:
The set of overlapping n-word windows of the lower-cased text (words split on whitespace).

A text with fewer than n words but at least one word gives a single shingle (all its
words); an empty text gives the empty set.

functions.name: jaccard
functions.doc: |A & B| / |A | B|, and 0.0 if both sets are empty.

functions.name: minhash_signature
functions.doc:
The MinHash signature: for each of the first `num_perm` hash functions
h_i(x) = (a_i * x + b_i) mod PRIME in HASH_COEFS, the minimum over the set of
h_i(base_hash(shingle)). An empty set gives [EMPTY] * num_perm.

functions.name: estimate_jaccard
functions.doc: The fraction of positions where two signatures agree.

milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand cases for shingles (three windows from seven words, lower-casing, any whitespace, fewer than n words gives one shingle, empty text gives the empty set) and Jaccard; signatures against an independent oracle of the definition; the union identity on random sets (a seeded check, so a failure names the seed); estimate accuracy over 40 random set pairs (mean error under 0.05); identical sets estimate to 1.0 and disjoint sets to about 0; and on the crawl, the mean error over the 43 duplicate pairs must stay under 0.05.
hints: Lower-case first, then text.lower().split(). A set comprehension over range(len(w) - n + 1) with " ".join(w[i:i+n]) gives the shingles.
Handle the two edge cases before the comprehension: no words, and fewer than n words.
The signature: hash every shingle once with base_hash, then for each (a, b) in HASH_COEFS[:num_perm] take min((a * x + b) % PRIME for x in xs).
An empty shingle set has no minimum: return [EMPTY] * num_perm.
The estimate is the fraction of equal positions.
milestones.solution:
def shingles(text, n=SHINGLE_WORDS):
    """The set of overlapping n-word windows of the lower-cased text (words split on whitespace).

    A text with fewer than n words but at least one word gives a single shingle (all its
    words); an empty text gives the empty set.
    """
    w = text.lower().split()
    if not w:
        return set()
    if len(w) < n:
        return {" ".join(w)}
    return {" ".join(w[i:i + n]) for i in range(len(w) - n + 1)}

def jaccard(a, b):
    """|A & B| / |A | B|, and 0.0 if both sets are empty."""
    union = len(a | b)
    return len(a & b) / union if union else 0.0

def minhash_signature(shingle_set, num_perm=NUM_PERM):
    """The MinHash signature: for each of the first `num_perm` hash functions
    h_i(x) = (a_i * x + b_i) mod PRIME in HASH_COEFS, the minimum over the set of
    h_i(base_hash(shingle)). An empty set gives [EMPTY] * num_perm."""
    if not shingle_set:
        return [EMPTY] * num_perm
    xs = [base_hash(s) for s in shingle_set]
    return [min((a * x + b) % PRIME for x in xs) for a, b in HASH_COEFS[:num_perm]]

def estimate_jaccard(sig_a, sig_b):
    """The fraction of positions where two signatures agree."""
    return sum(x == y for x, y in zip(sig_a, sig_b)) / len(sig_a)
milestones.explain:
Most duplicates on the web are not byte-identical. The same article appears with a changed header, a corrected word, an extra sentence. To find them you need a definition of "similar" and a way to avoid comparing every pair, because comparing every pair of N documents costs N²/2 comparisons, hopeless at web scale (chapter 1 works out 5 × 1019 for ten billion documents).

The definition first. Turn each document into its set of shingles, the overlapping runs of n consecutive words (FineWeb uses n = 5). The Jaccard similarity of two documents is the size of the overlap of their shingle sets divided by the size of their union:

J(A, B) = |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|

It is 1 for identical documents and 0 for documents sharing no five-word run. The shingle size is a real choice, and it is why a single changed word is not a single changed shingle: one edited word spoils up to n shingles around it. The following table (script exp_shingle.py, on three pairs from the crawl) shows the dial. Short shingles make unrelated pages look related because common phrases overlap; long shingles make a lightly edited copy look different:

$ python3 exp_shingle.py
  shingle  light edit  one sentence  unrelated   P(candidate) at 14 x 8, light edit
    2-word       0.827         0.767      0.099   0.97
    3-word       0.823         0.758      0.041   0.96
    5-word       0.757         0.747      0.013   0.80
    8-word       0.685         0.743      0.003   0.50
   12-word       0.605         0.737      0.000   0.23

Jaccard is easy to compute but still expensive: sets are large. MinHash (Broder, 1997) compresses each set into a short signature of numbers whose agreement rate estimates J. Choose a random hash function h on shingles and let the MinHash of a set be the smallest h value among its members. For two sets, the minimum over their union is attained by exactly one shingle; the two minima are equal precisely when that shingle lies in both sets, which happens with probability |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B| = J (chapter 1 gives the argument in full). With k independent hash functions, the fraction of positions where two signatures agree is an estimate of J with standard error √(J(1 − J)/k), about 0.04 for J = 0.75 and k = 112.

You do not need random permutations. The lab gives you a family of 112 functions hi(x) = (ai x + bi) mod p, with p = 261 − 1, applied to a 64-bit BLAKE2 hash of each shingle (HASH_COEFS, PRIME and base_hash in starter.py). Position i of the signature is the minimum of hi over the document's shingles. This has a property the checker uses as an exact test: the signature of a union is the position-wise minimum of the two signatures, because the minimum of a union is the smaller of the two minima. If your signatures obey that for random sets, you built MinHash and not something that merely looks like it.

How many hash functions? More buy a smaller error and cost storage and time per document. On the 43 duplicate pairs of the crawl (script exp_perm.py):

$ python3 exp_perm.py
43 duplicate pairs
num_perm  mean error   worst
       8       0.093   0.296
      16       0.073   0.240
      32       0.051   0.233
      64       0.043   0.155
     112       0.029   0.103
milestones.card:
Near-duplicate pages share most of their text but not all of it, so we score the overlap. A shingle is a run of n consecutive words; the similarity of two texts is the number of shingles they share divided by the number of distinct shingles in either.

shingles(text, n) returns the set of n-word windows of the lower-cased, whitespace-split text, and jaccard(a, b) is the similarity of two such sets. A signature compresses a set: each of the first num_perm pairs in HASH_COEFS is one hash function, applied to the base_hash of each shingle, and minhash_signature keeps each function's smallest value. For one function, the two minima agree exactly when the smallest hash over the union belongs to both sets, which has probability equal to the similarity. So estimate_jaccard is the fraction of positions where two signatures agree.

{x, y, z} against {y, z, w}: 2 shared, 4 in either, similarity 0.5
56 of 112 signature positions agree: estimate 0.5

milestones.solution:
def band_keys(sig, b=BANDS, r=ROWS):
    """Split a signature into b bands of r rows. Return b hashable keys, one per band,
    each of the form (band_index, tuple_of_the_r_values). The band index is part of the
    key so a match in band 3 never collides with a match in band 4."""
    return [(i, tuple(sig[i * r:(i + 1) * r])) for i in range(b)]

def candidate_pairs(sigs, b=BANDS, r=ROWS):
    """All pairs of documents that share at least one band.

    sigs: dict id -> signature (length at least b * r). Returns a set of tuples
    (id1, id2) with id1 < id2. Use one hash table from band key to the list of ids that
    have it; never compare two documents unless they landed in the same bucket.
    """
    buckets = {}
    for doc_id, sig in sigs.items():
        for key in band_keys(sig, b, r):
            buckets.setdefault(key, []).append(doc_id)
    pairs = set()
    for ids in buckets.values():
        for i in range(len(ids)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(ids)):
                pairs.add((min(ids[i], ids[j]), max(ids[i], ids[j])))
    return pairs

def candidate_probability(s, b=BANDS, r=ROWS):
    """P(two documents of Jaccard similarity s become a candidate pair) = 1 - (1 - s^r)^b."""
    return 1.0 - (1.0 - s ** r) ** b

def threshold(b=BANDS, r=ROWS):
    """The similarity at which the S-curve is steepest, approximately (1/b)^(1/r)."""
    return (1.0 / b) ** (1.0 / r)

def best_bands(num_perm, target):
    """Among all (b, r) with b * r == num_perm, the one whose threshold(b, r) is closest to `target`.
    Returns (b, r). If two are equally close, prefer the one with more bands."""
    options = [(b, num_perm // b) for b in range(1, num_perm + 1) if num_perm % b == 0]
    return min(options, key=lambda br: (abs(threshold(*br) - target), -br[0]))
milestones.explain:
Signatures make each comparison cheap, but there are still N²/2 of them. Locality-sensitive hashing (LSH) avoids almost all comparisons by arranging for similar documents to land in the same hash bucket. Split each signature of 112 numbers into b = 14 bands of r = 8 rows. Put each band's tuple of 8 values, together with the band's index, into a dictionary that maps it to the list of documents that have it. Two documents become a candidate pair if they agree on all 8 values of at least one band. Only documents sharing a bucket are ever looked at, so the cost scales with the number of near-duplicates, not with the number of pairs.

The arithmetic is short. A single signature position agrees with probability J (milestone 4). All r positions of one band agree with probability Jr. A band fails with probability 1 − Jr, all b bands fail with probability (1 − Jr)b, so

P(candidate) = 1 − (1 − Jr)b

This is an S-shaped curve in J and the banding is the dial that moves it. The steepest part sits near (1/b)1/r, which for 14 × 8 is 0.72, in line with FineWeb's stated aim of removing documents at least 75% similar. The figure and table show four ways to spend the same 112 numbers (computed with your candidate_probability and threshold from the solution, script exp_scurve.py):

$ python3 exp_scurve.py
similarity   7 x 16  14 x 8   28 x 4   56 x 2 
      0.10    0.000    0.000    0.003    0.430
      0.20    0.000    0.000    0.044    0.898
      0.30    0.000    0.001    0.204    0.995
      0.50    0.000    0.053    0.836    1.000
      0.60    0.002    0.211    0.979    1.000
      0.70    0.023    0.565    1.000    1.000
      0.75    0.068    0.772    1.000    1.000
      0.80    0.181    0.924    1.000    1.000
      0.90    0.762    1.000    1.000    1.000
threshold     0.885    0.719    0.435    0.134

Read the table across the 0.75 row. Seven bands of 16 rows would flag a 75%-similar pair only 7% of the time. Fourteen bands of 8 flag it 77% of the time, and a near-miss at 0.5 only 5% of the time. Fifty-six bands of 2 flag a pair at J = 0.3 with probability 0.995: that setting finds everything, and a great deal that is not a duplicate. Which of these is right depends on what happens next: if a verification step follows, favour recall and let it throw away the false alarms; if the candidates are merged blindly, favour precision.

The key implementation points are small but easy to get wrong. Include the band index in the bucket key, or a value that happens to repeat in band 3 of one document and band 4 of another is a false collision. Report each pair once, ordered. And never loop over all pairs: the checker builds 8,000 random signatures with 20 planted near-copies and gives you a few seconds, which an all-pairs comparison (32 million pairs) cannot meet.
milestones.card:
Comparing every pair of documents is far too slow. Instead, make similar documents land in the same bucket of a hash table and compare only those that share one: cut each document's signature (its list of numbers) into b bands of r values, and call two documents candidates if some band is identical in both.

band_keys(sig, b, r) returns one key per band, built from the band's index and its r values. candidate_pairs builds a dict from each key to the ids holding it; every pair inside one bucket is a candidate. Why this works: a band matches with probability s^r when two documents have similarity s, and all b bands miss with probability (1 - s^r)^b, so candidate_probability is one minus that. threshold is (1/b)^(1/r), where the curve is steepest. best_bands tries every split of num_perm into b times r and returns the one whose threshold is nearest the target.

similarity 0.5, 14 bands of 8: 0.5^8 = 0.0039 per band
P(candidate) = 1 - (1 - 0.0039)^14 = 0.053

Within a cluster keep the smallest id. run_pipeline returns the given Report.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. Hand cases for precision and recall (including the empty conventions) and for clusters (a chain, and pairs given in either order); a three-document near_dedupe; a pair that 56 × 2 merges but min_jaccard=0.6 separates; then the whole crawl: every page is kept or dropped exactly once, all spam, stubs and non-English pages are dropped at the quality stage, nothing is dropped as a copy of a different article, the six related pages survive, precision at 14 × 8 is at least 0.95 and recall at least 0.85, and across four banding settings recall rises as the threshold falls while 56 × 2 has precision under 0.8.
hints: Precision and recall: hit = len(predicted & gold), with the empty cases returning 1.0 for the empty denominator.

clusters: union-find with a parent dict and a find that follows parents to the root. Union the roots of each pair, then group the ids by root. Sort inside each group and sort the groups by their first id.

near_dedupe: shingle every text, sign every shingle set, call candidate_pairs, filter by the true Jaccard, and call clusters(sorted(docs), pairs). The kept id of a cluster is group[0]; every other member maps to it in removed.

run_pipeline: write it as a loop over the stages, filling Report as you go. For the evaluation, corpus.gold_pairs(ids) restricted to the documents that entered the near-duplicate stage is the right gold set.
milestones.solution:
def precision_recall(predicted, gold):
    """(precision, recall) of a set of predicted pairs against the gold set.

    precision = |predicted & gold| / |predicted|, recall = |predicted & gold| / |gold|.
    An empty prediction has precision 1.0 (it claimed nothing wrong); an empty gold set
    has recall 1.0.
    """
    hit = len(predicted & gold)
    return (hit / len(predicted) if predicted else 1.0), (hit / len(gold) if gold else 1.0)

def clusters(ids, pairs):
    """Connected components of the graph whose nodes are `ids` and edges are `pairs`.

    Returns a list of sorted id lists, sorted by their first id. An id in no pair is a
    cluster of one. (Union-find, or a simple graph search.)
    """
    parent = {i: i for i in ids}

    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]          # path halving
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    for a, b in pairs:
        ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
        if ra != rb:
            parent[max(ra, rb)] = min(ra, rb)
    groups = {}
    for i in ids:
        groups.setdefault(find(i), []).append(i)
    return sorted((sorted(g) for g in groups.values()), key=lambda g: g[0])

def near_dedupe(docs, b=BANDS, r=ROWS, min_jaccard=0.0):
    """Remove near-duplicates with MinHash and LSH.

    docs: dict id -> text. Steps: shingle every text, sign it, find candidate pairs with
    `candidate_pairs`, then keep only the candidates whose TRUE Jaccard similarity is at
    least `min_jaccard` (0.0 keeps them all). Group the surviving pairs into clusters and
    keep the smallest id of each cluster.

    Returns (kept_ids, removed, pairs): kept_ids a sorted list, removed a dict mapping each
    removed id to the cluster representative that was kept, pairs the set of pairs used.
    """
    sh = {i: shingles(t) for i, t in docs.items()}
    sigs = {i: minhash_signature(s) for i, s in sh.items()}
    pairs = {p for p in candidate_pairs(sigs, b, r) if jaccard(sh[p[0]], sh[p[1]]) >= min_jaccard}
    kept, removed = [], {}
    for group in clusters(sorted(docs), pairs):
        kept.append(group[0])
        for other in group[1:]:
            removed[other] = group[0]
    return sorted(kept), removed, pairs

def run_pipeline(pages, b=BANDS, r=ROWS):
    """Run every stage on a list of corpus.Page and return a Report.

    Order: extract -> c4_line_filter(require_punct=False) -> quality_flags (drop pages with
    any flag; dropped[id] = ("quality", ",".join(flags))) -> line_dedupe -> exact_dedupe
    (dropped[id] = ("exact", kept_id)) -> near_dedupe (dropped[id] = ("near", kept_id)).
    `after_lines` is the number of documents still non-empty after line_dedupe (empty ones
    are dropped as ("lines", "empty")). `precision` and `recall` score near_dedupe's pairs
    against corpus.gold_pairs of the documents that entered it.
    """
    rep = Report(n_pages=len(pages))
    docs = []
    for p in pages:
        text = c4_line_filter(extract(p.html), require_punct=False)
        flags = quality_flags(text)
        if flags:
            rep.dropped[p.id] = ("quality", ",".join(flags))
        else:
            docs.append((p.id, text))
    rep.after_quality = len(docs)
    docs = line_dedupe(docs)
    for i, t in docs:
        if not t:
            rep.dropped[i] = ("lines", "empty")
    docs = [(i, t) for i, t in docs if t]
    rep.after_lines = len(docs)
    docs, exact_dropped = exact_dedupe(docs)
    for i, rep_id in exact_dropped.items():
        rep.dropped[i] = ("exact", rep_id)
    rep.after_exact = len(docs)
    kept, removed, pairs = near_dedupe(dict(docs), b, r)
    for i, rep_id in removed.items():
        rep.dropped[i] = ("near", rep_id)
    rep.kept, rep.after_near, rep.candidates = kept, len(kept), len(pairs)
    rep.precision, rep.recall = precision_recall(pairs, corpus.gold_pairs({i for i, _ in docs}))
    return rep
milestones.explain:
A deduplicator makes two kinds of mistake. It can miss a duplicate, which leaves repeated text in the corpus, and it can merge two pages that are only similar, which throws away text you wanted. Measure both against the labelled duplicate pairs (the pairs of pages in corpus.gold_pairs, which share a family):

  • Precision = reported true pairs / reported pairs: of the pairs you claimed were duplicates, how many are?
  • Recall = reported true pairs / true pairs: of the real duplicate pairs, how many did you find?

(The same pair of numbers appears in retrieval evaluation and in imbalanced classification; it is the same trade-off wearing different clothes.) Pairs are not yet a corpus. To remove duplicates you group the pairs into clusters, the connected components of the graph whose edges are the pairs (union-find does it in a dozen lines), and keep one document per cluster. Because components are transitive, one wrong pair can chain two whole families into a single cluster and delete one of them, which is why the precision of the candidate pairs matters more than a pair-level percentage suggests.

The reference pipeline runs these stages in order: extract; C4 line filter with the punctuation rule off; quality flags; line deduplication; exact deduplication; near-duplicate removal. Each dropped page is recorded with the stage and a reason, so nothing disappears without an explanation. Here is its funnel on the crawl (script exp_funnel.py):

$ python3 exp_funnel.py
118 pages -> 87 after quality -> 87 after line dedupe -> 73 after exact -> 50 after near-duplicates

dropped at quality : borderline 3, nonenglish 8, short 8, spam 12
dropped at exact   : article 8, exact 6
dropped at near    : article 5, exact 2, light 9, medium 7
kept            : article 27, exact 6, light 4, medium 3, related 6, seo 4

near-duplicate pairs: precision 1.00, recall 0.96

31 pages leave at the quality stage: 28 spam, stub and non-English pages and the 3 short good notes. The exact stage removes 14 pages, one for each generated copy, once line deduplication has removed the promotional lines. The near-duplicate stage removes 23 more, and the survivors hold exactly one version of every one of the 40 articles, plus the six related pages that quote an article without copying it, plus four keyword-stuffed pages that no rule could see. Precision is 1.00 and recall 0.96: of the 26 duplicate pairs left after exact deduplication, 25 were found.

The default is one point on a curve. Sweeping the banding (script exp_sweep.py) shows the whole trade-off, including what a bad choice costs:

$ python3 exp_sweep.py
   b x r thresh pairs precision recall  left  wrongly removed
  4 x 28    0.95     1      1.00   0.04    72                0
  7 x 16    0.89     9      1.00   0.35    64                0
  8 x 14    0.86    16      1.00   0.62    57                0
 14 x 8     0.72    25      1.00   0.96    50                0
 16 x 7     0.67    25      1.00   0.96    50                0
 28 x 4     0.43    27      0.96   1.00    49                1
 56 x 2     0.13    50      0.52   1.00    40               13

At 7 × 16 the detector is conservative and finds only a third of the duplicates, leaving 64 documents. At 14 × 8 it is almost perfect. At 56 × 2 it flags 50 pairs of which only about half are real, and the last column shows the damage: thirteen pages removed that were not copies of their cluster's representative. A one-line change to the banding turned a deduplicator into a deleter of unique text.
milestones.card:
A deduplicator can miss real duplicates or merge pages that are merely similar; precision (the share of reported pairs that are real) and recall (the share of real pairs reported) count the two mistakes. Reported pairs then form clusters, groups linked by any chain of pairs, and one page survives per cluster.

precision_recall(predicted, gold) compares two sets of pairs. clusters(ids, pairs) finds the connected groups: pairs chain, whichever way round each is written, so a union-find or a graph search does it. near_dedupe chains the given helpers (shingles, minhash_signature, candidate_pairs, jaccard) with your clusters. It drops candidates whose true similarity is below min_jaccard and keeps the smallest id of each cluster. run_pipeline calls the stages in the docstring's order and records every drop with its stage, so each page is either kept or dropped, exactly once.

predicted {ab, bc}, real {ab, bc, cd, ef}: precision 2/2, recall 2/4
clusters(["a","b","c","d"], [("a","b"), ("c","b")]) = [["a","b","c"], ["d"]]
